author: Australian Associated Press
description:
Officers searched a Mount Waverley home in Melbourne after trophies belonging to winning horse Makybe Diva were stolen from Flemington racecourse

  • Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

A police raid has failed to locate three Melbourne Cup trophies belonging to champion horse Makybe Diva after a smash and grab at Flemington racecourse.

A Mount Waverley home in Melbourne’s east was raided on Monday evening after thieves smashed their way into a glass display case at the racecourse about 6.30am.

Continue reading...
title: Police searching for three stolen Melbourne Cup trophies worth $1m each

author: Maya Yang
description:
Police investigation continues even as Louisiana coroner’s office releases findings on death of Kenan ‘Ken’ Urker

The cause of death of Gypsy Rose Blanchard’s partner, who died last month, has been released.

On Monday, the Lafourche parish coroner’s office in Louisiana determined that Kenan “Ken” Urker, 34, died from accidental polysubstance drug toxicity on 1 October, USA Today reports. The coroner’s office also said the case is complete.

Continue reading...
title: Cause of death released for partner of Gypsy Rose Blanchard

author: Agence France-Presse and Press Association
description:
• Jürgen Klopp’s side make statement with 5-0 triumph

  • Dutch advance, Greece miss out despite win over Serbia

Florian Wirtz scored twice as Germany delivered a 5-0 rout of the Netherlands in Berlin on Monday, reaching the Nations League quarter-finals as group winners.

Brajan Gruda contributed a goal and two assists, with Derry Scherhant and Nico Schlotterbeck also on the scoresheet as the hosts delivered their most impressive display so far under Jürgen Klopp’s leadership.

Continue reading...
title: Nations League: Wirtz doubles up as Germany rout Netherlands to top group

author: Lois Beckett
description:
Fans of the sport dubbed the event ‘Monster Day’ as pro surfers tackled the storm-driven waves at Mavericks Beach

While this year’s Super El Niño storms are battering the California coast and destroying homes and infrastructure, surfers are finding a silver lining: waves so epic that pro athletes from around the world are making last-minute journeys to experience them.

Big wave surfers converged on northern California this Saturday to ride massive, storm-driven swells at the famously dangerous Mavericks Beach, an event some surf fans called “Monster Day.”

Continue reading...
title: Big wave surfers line up to ride ‘raw power of the Pacific’ during Super El-Niño swells

author: Guardian sport and agencies
description:
• USA beat Canada 6-2 to claim 12th world title

  • Knight and Pannek score twice each in victory

  • United States 6-2 Canada – as it happened

The United States beat Canada 6-2 on Monday to win the women’s ice hockey world championship in Herning, Denmark, becoming the first US team to capture Olympic and world titles in the same calendar year.

Hilary Knight and Kelly Pannek scored twice each as the Americans claimed their 12th world championship, adding to the Olympic gold medal they won in Milan in February. Lacey Eden also scored for the US, while Sarah Fillier had both goals
title: USA thrash Canada to win women’s hockey worlds and complete historic golden double

author: Johana Bhuiyan
description:
Latent bug or defect from July caused Microsoft’s servers to ‘become overwhelmed and unresponsive’, executive says

Microsoft has identified the root cause of the outage on Thursday that crippled Outlook, Exchange and a host of other vital office software across the globe.

The company issued an initial report on Monday that identified a months-old bug malfunctioning connections between internal systems as the factors that led to the 24-hour blackout of Microsoft services. Each of these factors may have easily been resolved on their own but, together, led to a major outage that was harder to mitigate, company executives said.

Continue reading...
title: Microsoft identifies months-old bug as root cause of global outage

author: Rajeev Syal Home affairs editor
description:
Home Office plans condemned as ‘distressing’ by refugee charities

Asylum seekers who have exhausted the formal appeals process will be stripped of a five-day grace period and become eligible for immediate removal under Home Office plans condemned as “distressing” by refugee charities.

Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, will amend a bill currently before parliament to allow Immigration Enforcement officers to detain and remove people who have unsuccessfully appealed against their asylum or immigration claim being rejected without further notice.

Continue reading...
title: Failed UK asylum seekers to lose five-day grace period and face immediate removal

author: Sam Levin
description:
Lizbeth Vargas Andrade, 23, was taken down by officers and arrested on her stomach during a protest, her attorney says

US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents pepper-sprayed a pregnant US citizen and threw her to the ground during a protest in California on Sunday, according to her family’s attorney, who shared footage of the incident.

Lizbeth Vargas Andrade, 23, was filming and protesting the presence of several ICE officers outside the Stanislaus county jail in Modesto, in California’s central valley, before she was taken down by officers and arrested on her stomach during a chaotic encounter.

Continue reading...
title: ICE agents pepper spray pregnant US citizen in California, video shows

author: Emma Madden
description:
All of Hollywood’s biggest stars are in attendance for the Governors’ awards, but nobody gets drunk and the biggest draw is an awkward documentarian

Timothée Chalamet was seconds away from getting into trouble. It was just after 6pm in Hollywood and Lynette Howell Taylor, president of the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences, was trying to corral a crowd of 700-odd people into sitting down so she could begin the Governors awards ceremony. She jokingly threatened to start calling out anyone still standing by name if they didn’t sit down imminently. Chalamet was the only one left on his feet, circling the table where he was due to sit next to his girlfriend, Kylie Jenner, opposite Tom Holland and Zendaya. Howell Taylor gave him a few seconds’ grace. He looked like the popular kid testing how far he could push a headteacher.

The Governors awards had a curiously school-like atmosphere this year. Even the carpet in the Ray Dolby Ballroom was faded and striped. The soc
title: Glenn Close cries! John Malkovich weeps! But it’s Nathan Fielder everyone wants to talk to at the honorary Oscars

author: Editorial
description:
Predicting a final destination for reset negotiations between the EU and the UK is futile, given the wider challenges that Brussels is facing

At the European Political Community summit in Dublin last week, Emmanuel Macron was pictured apparently waving a grinning Andy Burnham to a seat at the head of the table, as Ursula von der Leyen, the European Commission president, looked on. It was the visual equivalent of the “welcome back” message delivered by the French president in the early autumn, following Mr Burnham’s suggestion that rejoining the EU was an option for the UK to consider. At the time, Le Monde was among the media outlets to try out an updated portmanteau to mark the moment; mercifully, “
title: The Guardian view on Europe and Burnham: a future that can only be viewed through a glass darkly | Editorial

author: Editorial
description:
From Welsh rugby to English football, victories on the pitch can capture a nation’s imagination and briefly make the impossible seem possible

The world divides roughly in two: people who like sport and people who don’t see the point. George Orwell was roundly dismissive – “war minus the shooting”. Adrian Conan Doyle (Sir Arthur’s son) had the super-rationalist Sherlock Holmes baffled by why anyone should care that one horse could outrun another. Yet sport can do something that life rarely does: offer a comprehensible narrative, with a beginning, a middle and, gloriously, an end. Life is convoluted, messy and ultimately hard to assess; sport can offer resolution in 80 or 90 minutes. All of which is a long-winded way of saying: weren’t Wales
title: The Guardian view on sporting triumphs: more than just a game | Editorial

author: Nadia Khomami Arts and culture correspondent
description:
The 40-year-old British actor has had a remarkable career and is back again with the coveted 007

  • New James Bond announced ... and the name’s Pattinson, Robert Pattinson

  • Robert Pattinson’s gift for cool, sensual menace makes him an exquisite choice as James Bond

There are big years in an actor’s career, and then there is Robert Pattinson’s 2026.

This year the 40-year-old Briton has been the face of everything from Kristoffer Borgli’s relationship satire The Drama to Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey and Lance Oppenheim’s Primetime. Now, in the culmination of a remarkable run, he has landed the most coveted role in British cinema: James Bond.
title: Robert Pattinson’s journey from Harry Potter and Twilight to James Bond: ‘The honour of a lifetime’

author: Zoe Williams
description:
The understanding of refugees as complex individuals, motivated variously by wanting to build a new life and return to what was theirs, often seems to have been lost. A new film offers a different, truer, perspective

There was a screening last week of Seize the Summit, which follows four refugees as they try to reach the top of Kilimanjaro. It was organised by a recent MA graduate from Goldsmiths, with a panel afterwards, which I was set to chair. So she and I were spitballing what the film-maker, Arwa Damon, would want to talk about, and Hanya, the graduate, said: “I think her purpose is to mainstream the idea of the refugee as a human being.” It was such a stark statement that we both started laughing.

There are many categories of refugee in current affairs storytelling. There’s the desperate victim; the criminal, or criminal-waiting-to-happen; the hero, battling unimaginable odds, though this tends to be a retrospective narrative, ie second-generation members of a di
title: Hero, villain or victim: why are refugees so rarely seen now as fully human? | Zoe Williams

author: Jennifer Rankin in Brussels
description:
Germany, Austria, Netherlands, Denmark and Greece likely to face challenges to policy criticised as ‘grave moral failing’

Five EU member states have announced plans to set up an offshore centre in Rwanda for people with no legal right to stay in Europe, in a pilot scheme that is expected to face legal challenges and has been denounced as “a grave moral failing”.

The five countries – Germany, Austria, the Netherlands, Denmark and Greece – are the first to seek to use the EU’s newly agreed returns law that allows people who have exhausted all avenues of appeal against their removal from Europe to be sent to a third country.

Continue reading...
title: Five EU states announce plans for immigration ‘return hubs’ in Rwanda

author: Graham Readfearn in Antalya
description:
While mostly accurate describing simple facts, models pivoted to denial and wrong answers when challenged

  • Cop31 live – latest updates

Artificial intelligence models can quickly turn into climate crisis deniers at the mildest challenge from users, according to a new UN-backed study.

While AI models can accurately confirm simple facts about climate change, eight times out of 10 when they pivoted to a wrong answer, they did so “at the very first sign that the user mildly disagreed” to confirm incorrect statements such as “CO2 is not the main driver of climate change”.

Continue reading...
title: AI models ‘weak and fallible’ on climate science, UN-backed study reports

author: Oliver Milman
description:
‘Hyperscaler’ datacenters across country draw upon dirtier power sources to meet vast energy needs, research shows

The frantic buildout of “hyperscaler” datacenters in the US has collectively caused planet-heating emissions of about the same scale as Denmark emits in a year, new research has found.

In that period 403 “hyperscalers” – the largest datacenters used primarily to handle the growth of artificial intelligence – emitted about 25.7m metric tons of carbon dioxide, according to the study.

Continue reading...
title: Surge of US datacenters adds equivalent of Denmark’s annual emissions, study finds

author: Guardian community team
description:
As Daniel Craig’s successor as cinema’s favourite master spy is unveiled, we would like to hear your response, whether you are shaken or stirred

After years of speculation and many screen tests, Robert Pattinson has been announced as the next James Bond.

Denis Villeneuve, known for the Dune trilogy and Prisoners, is set to direct the new Bond film. This choice has led many to suspect this incarnation will be more gritty and serious than the earlier, more tongue-in-cheek outings by Roger Moore and Sean Connery.

Continue reading...
title: Share your thoughts on Robert Pattinson’s casting as the new James Bond

author: Neha Gohil Midlands correspondent
description:
Pair due to appear in court in December in relation to incident in May that left a man in his 30s with leg injuries

Two men have been charged following an incident in Birmingham, where a man was run over by a van after flags were removed from lamp-posts.

A man in his 30s was taken to hospital with leg injuries after the incident on Mayfield Road in the suburb of Stirchley, south-west Birmingham, on 14 May.

Continue reading...
title: Two charged after man run over by van during flags incident in Birmingham

author: Anna Betts in New York
description:
Mayor axes strategic response group that cracked down on protesters and announces new community safety division

Zohran Mamdani, New York City’s mayor, announced Monday that he was disbanding a controversial city police unit that has faced criticism over the years from civil rights groups who have accused the unit of using excessive force and unduly aggressive tactics against protesters.

In a video released Monday morning, Mamdani said the move stemmed from a campaign pledge he made to disband the New York City police department’s strategic response group (SRG). “Today, we are keeping that promise,” Mamdani said in the video.
title: Mamdani disbands controversial NYPD unit accused of using excessive force

author: Benjamin Lee
description:
The race is led by a number of female artists, also including Phoebe Bridgers and Ella Langley, with Beyoncé receiving her record-breaking 100th nomination

  • Grammys 2027: the nominations in all the major categories

Raye is leading this year’s female-heavy Grammys race with 11 nominations.

The British singer-songwriter, who has received four nominations in the past, picked up nods in categories including song of the year, songwriter of the year and album of the year.

Continue reading...
title: Grammys 2027: Raye, Rosalía and Olivia Rodrigo lead female-heavy nominations

author: Interviews by Michael Hogan
description:
‘When Jill and Glen are in bed, that was Steve Coogan’s bed. He was rarely there so we didn’t bother washing the sheets afterwards’

It all started with the character of Jill Tyrell. I’d done Human Remains a black comedy about oddball couples] with Rob Brydon and was trying to write something of my own. I remembered this woman from Human Remains called Beverley. She was in her 50s, from the West Country and did home hairdressing. She told a client: “The ammonia will burn your ears a bit, Joyce, that’s completely natural.” Bath and Bristol are embedded in my history, so I thought I’d develop that. I made Jill two decades younger and gave her husband Terry cancer, which she uses to her advantage.

Continue reading...
title: ‘George Michael came out of his coma talking like Jill’: Julia Davis and Rebecca Front on their squirm-inducing comedy Nighty Night

author: Rajeev Syal and Peter Walker
description:
PM’s spokesperson calls message, read out by convicted rapist’s wife on their YouTube channel, ‘clearly appalling’

The Ministry of Justice has launched an investigation into whether Russell Brand has broken prison rules after the jailed comedian shared a message claiming he is not guilty of sexual offences just days after his conviction.

Brand’s wife, Laura Brand, read a message from her rapist husband in a video uploaded to their YouTube channel in which he claimed: “I am not guilty of the offences I have been jailed for.”

Continue reading...
title: Ministry of Justice investigating Russell Brand message from prison claiming he is not guilty

author: Chris Wiegand
description:
Luke Sheppard’s revival of Andrew Lloyd Webber’s 80s musical is in cinemas and going on tour. What gives these ridiculous, rollerskating trains such emotional force?

I hardly ever cry at the theatre but can think of three recent cases. 1. The beautifully jittery balcony scene in Liverpool Everyman’s Romeo and Juliet. 2. Dear Theodosia as co-sung by Leslie Odom Jr (actual OG Aaron Burr!) in Hamilton. 3. An embarrassingly large amount of Starlight Express.

Why on earth does this ridiculous fantasy of rollerskating trains, with their high-speed scrapes, leave me feeling like an em
title: Souped-up and now on screen, Starlight Express is moving in all sorts of ways

author: Imran Lodhi, as told to Morgan Krakow
description:
When the floods hit Pakistan he went out to help. Then the water reached his own family. This is Imran Lodhi’s story

Location: Dera Ghazi Khan, Pakistan

Disaster: Pakistan intense monsoon rainfall

Imran Lodhi is a university lecturer with a doctorate in climate change and sustainable development. The 41-year-old was living in Dera Ghazi Khan, a city in south-western Punjab, when floods devastated provinces across Pakistan. Climate change made the monsoon rainfall that caused the floods more intense.

Continue reading...
title: ‘When the sun came out it felt like it opened a scar’ – This is climate breakdown

author: Alexandra Villarreal
description:
Attorneys say federal officials are expediting immigration hearings and exhausting legal tools to prioritize mass deportations without any semblance of due process

Four days. That’s all the notice that the New Orleans immigration court gave attorney Corinne Beth to get a family of six ready to defend their asylum case to stay in the US, an intensive process that lawyers estimate requires at least 50 to 75 hours of dedicated preparation.

The court had already brought forward the family’s next hearing once, from a date in July 2028, saying that it was “a priority case” and must be completed by the end of November without explaining why.

Continue reading...
title: ‘No rhyme or reason’: how Trump’s immigration courts put families on a fast track to deportation

author: Claudia Geib with visuals by Tony Luong
description:
The unfamiliar mollusk first turned up in this harvester’s haul in 2023. He asked a scientist to identify it, and together they realized they were seeing a potentially harmful, non-native species

Shellfish harvester Ernie Eldredge is on the hunt for clams, ankle-deep in water amid a landscape that’s almost desert-like in the wake of the receding tide. He runs his rake through fine white sand again and again without hearing the faint “clink” of its tines hitting a shell.

Eldredge just shrugs and moves on to the next spot. These tidal flats, perched on the elbow of Cape Cod in Chatham, Massachusetts, are constantly changing. Recent fall winds have carried a lot more sand into the area, and Eldredge thinks the clams he was finding over the summer may have moved on.

Continue reading...
title: Working in Cape Cod’s waters, he saw a unusual clam. It was the start of an invasion

author: Daniel Harris
description:
• ATP Finals group stage updates from the 1pm GMT start

  • Andreeva wins WTA Finals | And you can email Daniel

It was hard not to feel some level of relief when Carlos Alcaraz lost a five-set epic to Ben Shelton at the US Open because, after missing almost five months and two majors with what must’ve been a fairly significant wrist injury, for him to immediately reassert by taking his first tournament back, despite not being at full power, would not have spoken well of the game.

On the other hand, he has important and pressing tennising to do; while he was away and settling back in, Jannik Sinner unwell in Paris, hurt his knee at Wimbledon and took the rest of the year off to recover. This left a power vacuum at the top of the men’s game which Alexander Zverev, hitherto unable t
title: Carlos Alcaraz v Frances Tiafoe: ATP Finals tennis group stage – live

author: Jillian Ambrose
description:
Subsidy scheme, which is paid via taxes and energy bills, must be reformed, ECU analysis finds

  • Business live – latest updates

Great Britain’s oldest renewable energy projects are likely to rake in an almost £9bn windfall next year because of soaring market prices, according to independent analysis.

The research has revealed that almost a third of the UK’s wind and solar farms that rely on the government’s legacy renewables subsidy scheme are in line for surging subsidy payments as officials grapple with plans to lower the country’s energy costs.

Continue reading...
title: Great Britain’s oldest renewables projects could rake in nearly £9bn next year

author: Matt Hughes
description:
• Global cricket tournaments will avoid March to May

  • IPL expected to expand to 12 teams from 2028

Jay Shah has been re-elected unopposed as chair of the International Cricket Council after a board meeting in Bali that has also paved the way for the expansion of the Indian Premier League. In announcing their major events schedule until 2035, the ICC has moved all of their global tournaments to the second half of the year, creating a three-month period, from March to May, that is expected to be filled by the IPL.

In the past two years, the men’s T20 World Cup and Champions Trophy have been played in February and March. The Future Tours Programme governing bilateral series between ICC members has yet to be signed off, but sources involved in those discussions have indicated that no major series will be scheduled during those months.

Continue read
title: Jay Shah re-elected unopposed as ICC chair after board clears way for bigger IPL

author: Sam Leith
description:
Mortimer’s off-kilter charm energises the story of a troubled teenager in 1970s Middlesbrough

In comedian Bob Mortimer’s fourth novel, Michael, when we meet him, isn’t an angel; but he’s in a place that he suspects is at least angel-adjacent. He’s dead, or close to it, having come round from an emergency heart bypass in his 52nd year only to find himself sinking into a deep pool of warm gloop with honey-coloured light flowing at him from all directions. A disembodied voice calling itself Charles has offered him a choice that is hinted at but so far unspecified. What we do know is that before he makes his choice, Michael – a rock star who had three Top 10 hits in the UK and once danced in an LA disco with Björk and Courtney Love – is invited to revisit a single year of his life. He lands, somewhat trepidatiously, on the year he turned 14.

So back down memory lane we amble, the mysterious and otherworldly frame story intruding only in brief chapte
title: Michael by Bob Mortimer review – heartwarming quirkiness from the comedian

author: Robert Tait in Washington
description:
Experts say US president may lean toward global affairs after domestic influence curtailed in midterm elections

Donald Trump is embarking on his first overseas trip since his Republican party’s thumping midterm repudiation by US voters, in what may herald a renewed focus on foreign policy for the remainder of his presidency.

The US president will meet his Chinese and Russian counterparts Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin for their first trilateral summit, on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) forum in the Chinese city of Shenzhen. Before that, he will land in Manila in the Philippines on Tuesday for the Association of South-east Asian Nations (Asean) summit.

Continue reading...
title: Trump to embark on Asia trip in apparent foreign policy push before end of term

author: Osita Nwanevu
description:
Americans are at a real point of decision – not election day, but this heady, uncertain moment after

Until 2026, the most important midterm year of the last quarter-century was very probably 2010. Barack Obama famously called the elections a “shellacking” for the Democratic party and he was right. Thanks to a sluggish economic recovery from the Great Recession and backlash to the passage of the Affordable Care Act, Republicans took control of the House with a 63-seat gain – the largest House sweep since the 1940s – and won six seats in the Senate.

But the 2010 midterms were significant well beyond those numbers. It was the first election shaped by the rise of
title: The Democratic party is at a critical crossroad. Can it do the right thing? | Osita Nwanevu

author: Georgina Lawton
description:
I was stressed and newly diagnosed with ADHD when I decided to choose a new hobby. It awakened my playfulness and immediately improved my quality of life

In 2024, I decided to return to England after four and a half years in Lisbon. My first winter back in the UK was psychologically challenging. Working alone on my next book didn’t feel as enjoyable in cold, grey London as it had abroad. The 10th anniversary of my father’s death was approaching and I felt a profound loneliness which, much like the cold, began to seep into my bones. I was struggling, too, to readjust to London’s cost and pace of living.

During this time, I was diagnosed with combined-type attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). I used to think I was depressed, but my diagnosis made me realise that part of how I felt was burnout – my brain’s ability to regulate stress was depleted. I felt overwhelmed and would shut down, which would lead to cycles of anxiety, depression and self-criticism.
title: The one change that worked: I was burnt out and lonely – until I started ice skating

author: David Smith in Washington
description:
Filipino-US journalist Maria Ressa’s new book is a cri de coeur against the twin threats of authoritarianism and tech oligarchy – and how we can fight back

Maria Ressa keeps apologising. “Sorry, I’m hyper, too much coffee!” she says at one point. “Sorry, I can rant for a long time, so you have to stop me!” she says at another.

Ressa can be forgiven for firing on all cylinders. The Nobel peace prize laureate has just been to a screening in Britain of The Social Reckoning, which offers an unflattering portrayal of the tech titan Mark Zuckerberg, a man she regards as a “dictator”. Now she is speaking to the Guardian at a hotel in Washington’s Dupont Circle a few days before Americans vote in critical midterm elections.

Continue reading...
title: ‘Two dictators in my story – Duterte and Zuckerberg’: Nobel peace prize winner’s warning for democracy

author: Emma Beddington
description:
A psychologist has recommended we all take time for slowness and rest, to prepare ourselves for the coming months. It’s a nice idea, but it may prove my downfall

How are you feeling about the rapid dying of the light? Are you already sluggish and glum, poleaxed by the “polar vortex” or seasonal lurgy? That might be because you’re doing winter wrong: according to health psychologist Kari Leibowitz, writing in the Washington Post, we’d all benefit from a “winter transition week”.

Leibowitz, the author of a book, How to Winter, based on her time living in the Arctic, explains: “I intentionally
title: Not ready for the cold and dark? Maybe you need a ‘winter transition week’ | Emma Beddington

author: Harry Davies and Yuval Abraham
description:
Upload came as the Israeli military was increasing its reliance on Amazon’s cloud platform to meet the technological demands of its bombardment of Gaza

The Israeli military uploaded 3.5m photos to Amazon’s cloud platform in order to use the US company’s facial recognition technology to analyse images of Palestinians, the Guardian can reveal.

Leaked documents show the expansive catalogue of images was moved into Amazon’s cloud in the early months of Israel’s devastating aerial bombardment and ground offensive in Gaza.

Continue reading...
title: Revealed: Israel uploaded millions of photos to Amazon’s facial recognition platform to track Palestinians

author: Camilla Balshaw
description:
Reared on a puppy farm, and abandoned by a previous owner, he was half-starved when we adopted him. But he grew strong, chomping through everything from dog beds to sunglasses and my debut book

The day we brought our 14-week-old cocker spaniel home in 2022, I was wearing a silk scarf I’d picked up decades ago in a vintage shop in Tokyo. I didn’t know it then but that rainy afternoon would be the last time I’d wear it. Three days later, it was in my new puppy’s mouth. Once he’d finished tearing my scarf to shreds, he gazed at me with soulful chocolate brown eyes, fluttering his long eyelashes.

No matter how fond I was of that silk scarf, how could I be angry? Puppies chew stuff. That’s what they do. Mr Baxter gnawed his way through four dog beds, blankets and multiple dog leads. Nothing was off-limits. Socks, shoes, trainers, gloves, flat caps, berets, the freshly printed chapters of my debut book, a nifty pair of 70s sunglasses. Fearless and lithe, he grabbed things we
title: The pet I’ll never forget: Mr Baxter, who ate our belongings – and broke our hearts

author: Susan Chenery
description:
Sita Kali was involved in care for two of four babies who died between 2022 and 2024 in Lismore after free births or home births

  • Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

A self-described birth keeper advised a pregnant woman whose baby later died to “go home and rest” after she was given urgent medical advice to present to an emergency department, the New South Wales coroner’s court has heard.

Sita Tara Kali was involved in the care of two of four babies born in free births or home births who died in the northern rivers region between 2022 and 2024. An inquest into the deaths began in the Lismore local court on Monday. The families of the four babies were not present.
title: Birth keeper told mother of baby who later died to ‘go home and rest’, NSW inquest hears

author: Tracy McVeigh
description:
In this week’s newsletter: what the death of Cheikh Hamidou Kane reveals about the cultural gap, plus Iran’s rising use of executions to curb dissent

After reading about the death of the Senegalese writer Cheikh Hamidou Kane this week, I went on a mission to find his most famous book.

Described as a master of the pan-African novel and a literary giant, the 98-year-old received obituaries internationally, and in both French- and English-language African media. Le Monde called him “iconic”. His 1961 book L’Aventure Ambiguë (Ambiguous Adventure) has been studied in numerous universities and schools across the continent and is said to be one of the best books by an African writer to capture the post-colonial struggle for identity in newly independent countries.

Continue reading...
title: After the death of a literary giant in Africa, why could I find no copies of his book?

author: Kevin Rawlinson
description:
Online service will be offered to patients with eligible conditions, in a first for a British high street pharmacy

Boots is to start prescribing medical cannabis, it has announced, in a first for a UK high street pharmacy.

The online service is being offered to patients in the UK aged 25 and older who have an eligible condition such as chronic pain, anxiety or insomnia.

Continue reading...
title: Boots to begin prescribing medical cannabis in UK

author: Graeme Wearden
description:
Rolling coverage of the latest economic and financial news

  • Elon Musk joins 165,000 others calling for Nvidia to bring back Jensen Huang in open letter

Britain’s main share index isn’t been dragged back by the AI sell-off.

The FTSE 100 share index rose by as much as 29 points, or 0.25%, to 10,931 points.

“London’s Footsie has started the week as a resilient player despite the risk-off sentiment reverberating amid the ongoing tech sell-off. The blue-chip index made tentative steps forward in early trade as its tech-lite nature makes it more insulated from the AI jitters. However, disappointing economic data from China and Japan, have raised global growth concerns and look set to hold back significant gains for the internationally focused index.

Mining stocks a
title: AI sell-off resumes as Jensen Huang ‘discusses comeback as Nvidia CEO’ – business live

author: Megan Davies for MetDesk
description:
Meanwhile, severe thunderstorms bring hailstones the size of baseballs in Argentina

The National Weather Service in the US has confirmed that an EF1 tornado touched down south-east of Newark in the Salem Woods neighbourhood, Delaware, on Thursday. The tornado reached 160 metres wide, had a path length of 4.4 miles (7.1km) and reached estimated peak winds of up to 100mph (161km/h). There were no injuries or fatalities but windows and roofs were damaged on several homes, a large hotel sign fell on to a number of cars, and a semi truck overturned on I95. Although Delaware often experiences a few tornadoes every year, this is only the second time the state has had tornado activity in November since 1950, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. The only other November tornado recorded was in 1989.

Severe storms have also resulted in tornadoes in Argentina as well as large hailstones. A round of severe thunderstorms moved through the central Córdoba
title: Delaware hit by rare November tornado

author: Ajit Niranjan
description:
Russia and Saudi Arabia among countries objecting to the traditional output text common in previous summits

It is a measure of how difficult a battle the Australian presidency of negotiations and the Turkish hosts of the conference face at Cop31 that, as the second week of talks begins, there are still deep divides not only as to what the outcome of this Cop should be, but even over what form it should take.

Deep into Saturday night, ahead of the official rest day on Sunday, negotiators from around the world were still slugging it out over whether this Cop should have a “cover decision”.

Continue reading...
title: Cop31 live: diplomats divided as climate crisis talks enter second week

author: Ben Child
description:
The adventurous weirdness of the Gunn/Safran era that fans responded to is now history. Can the DCU ever get back on track?

What was Warner Bros’ plan in 2022, when the studio decided to reboot its superhero output, jettison the increasingly muddled DC Extended Universe (DCEU) and replace it with a sparkling new DC Universe (DCU)? In part it was to wipe the slate clean after years of false starts, abandoned storylines and tonal lurches. There was a little bit of Marvel envy to proceedings, and quite possibly a desire to avoid having to ever again discuss Batman v Superman: Dawn of Justice’s numerous failings. But mostly it was to take advantage of hiring of a man whom nobody could accuse of being short of ideas on how to make comic book movies. To a greater or lesser extent, th
title: The DCU’s James Gunn and Peter Safran are out – this is the biggest disaster to hit superhero movies in years

author: Jean Coussins
description:
Telling people to set aside food, water and cash is all very well, but we need a truly joined-up resilience strategy – and we don’t have one

  • Jean Coussins is chair of the House of Lords national resilience committee

The public has been stocking up on bottled water, tinned food and wind-up radios since the government launched its Be Ready campaign last month. But it’s not the public’s willingness to prepare that should worry us. What’s missing is the government’s willingness to provide candid information about the escalating nature and frequency of the threats we face, and a coherent resilience plan that can be activated from the top of government to local, community and household levels.

In July, the then security minister, Angela Eagle, admitted to the House of Lords national resilience committee, of which I am chair
title: Prep for disaster, ministers said – and millions stocked up. It’s the UK government that’s not ready | Jean Coussins

author: Matthew Weaver
description:
Hackney mayor decries ‘assault’ on free speech over event featuring academic who is banned from entering UK

Shabana Mahmood has been accused of an “assault” on free speech over claims her officials tried to cancel an online talk by the climate academic Andreas Malm days after he was banned from entering the UK.

The event in Hackney, east London, was a launch party for the socialist magazine Tribune. It went ahead on 4 November in defiance of Home Office warnings.

Continue reading...
title: Home Office accused of trying to cancel online talk by Andreas Malm

author: Zoë Garbett
description:
As mayor, I intervened – but we should be alarmed the government is threatened by those passionately opposing genocide

  • Report: Home Office accused of trying to cancel online talk by Andreas Malm

Hackney is a place with a proud tradition of resistance. This is where anti-fascists stood up to Oswald Mosley’s Blackshirts, where women established a “peace camp” to protest against the rise of nuclear weapons, and where the movement against the poll tax helped to bring down Margaret Thatcher.

When I was elected mayor of Hackney in May, it was another chapter in this history: the first time
title: The Home Office tried to cancel a pro-Palestine event here in Hackney. Labour’s petty authoritarianism has gone too far | Zoë Garbett

author: Fiona Harvey in Antalya
description:
Exclusive: Experts say watering down ZEV mandate would slow market and hamper efforts to reduce cost of living

Moves to weaken the UK’s targets on electric vehicles would hurt the car industry as well as consumers, campaigners and experts have said before a key intervention from government advisers expected this week.

The climate change committee (CCC) will write to ministers on Wednesday about the effects of changing the zero emissions vehicle (ZEV) mandate on the cost of living and the UK’s net zero targets.

Continue reading...
title: Weakening UK electric vehicle targets would hurt car industry, ministers told

author: Tamlin Magee
description:
In 1961, a group of Italian creatives crossed the border to collect anti-Franco resistance songs and share them with the world – sparking intense backlash from the dictator. A new documentary retraces that perilous journey

In the summer of 1961, four Italians crossed the Pyrenees into fascist Spain. Unknown to the border guards, their car was loaded with microfilm, a tape recorder and, tucked in the pocket of a writer and musician named Sergio Liberovici, a book of matches – each split in half, etched with the addresses of Spanish antifascists in miniature and glued back together, a hairline fracture concealing secrets that, if discovered, could result in jail or worse.

Along with Michele Luciano Straniero, Emilio Jona and Margherita Galante Garrone, Liberovici was a member of a leftwing collective named Cantacronache. Formed in 1958 and counting Italo Calvino and Umberto Eco among their collaborators, the collective was repulsed by the superficiality of Italian pop mus
title: ‘A songbook for protest movements’: how did this secret mission to smuggle antifascist music out of Spain ever get forgotten?

author: Marie Mitchell
description:
Pucker up for squash and tamarind curry with stewed chickpeas and coriander, or how about whipped cannellini beans with leeks, roast radicchio and parmesan?

Who doesn’t love sweet and sour? If you’re complaining that you don’t right now, then you’re lying – it’s an almost perfect pairing. Here, I’m playing with the sweet-and-sour notes of vinegar and the tang of tamarind in two dishes that are on repeat in our house. Dinners for when you want to spend more time on the sofa and less time in the kitchen.

Continue reading...
title: Squash and chickpea curry, and whipped beans with radicchio: Marie Mitchell’s sweet-and-sour recipes

author: Oliver Milman in Antalya
description:
Proponents make renewed push for carbon dioxide removal (CDR) to be included in final text of Cop31

What happens when the world, as expected, hurtles dangerously past agreed temperature thresholds? At UN climate talks, countries are being urged to turn to technology to reverse this fate by sucking carbon directly from the atmosphere.

A renewed push by proponents of carbon dioxide removal (or CDR), where heat-trapping carbon dioxide is taken from the atmosphere and stored deep underground, in oceans or in products such as carbonated drinks, is seeking to gain recognition in the final text of Cop31, the climate summit currently under way in Antalya, Turkey.

Continue reading...
title: Efforts to suck carbon directly from atmosphere championed at UN climate talks

author: Fiona Harvey in Antalya
description:
Mia Mottley launches petition to reduce powerful greenhouse gas emissions as UN climate meeting enters second week

Staying silent on the climate crisis is pushing the world closer to disaster, the prime minister of Barbados, Mia Mottley, has said, urging people around the world to force a confrontation with politicians who are failing to do what is needed.

Taking action on methane emissions could be the emergency brake that gives the world time to decarbonise, Mottley said. She is urging people to sign a global petition to cut the powerful greenhouse gas.

Continue reading...
title: Barbados PM urges global citizens to demand methane cuts at Cop31 summit

author: Amelia Gentleman
description:
The head of Women’s Aid has a unique insight into the ways technology provides mechanisms for abuse. She discusses online predators, the UK’s early release scheme – and why the fastest growing cohort of domestic abusers is young men

At last Tuesday’s all-staff meeting for Women’s Aid there was an unfamiliar undercurrent of optimism. It is a feeling that is very unusual when you have about 85 people working in the domestic violence sector gathered in one room.

Staff were feeling encouraged by the sentencing of Russell Brand a day earlier, and also cheered by Channel 4’s announcement at the start of the month that it would stop making Married at First Sight, a programme the charity had campaigned against, calling out “multiple incidents where women have [been] subjected to abuse and manipulation” on these kinds of reality dating shows. In the breaks between meetings, employees were following the breaking news about sexual misconduct allegations against David Walliams.
title: Darker pornography, deepfakes and chemical coercion: Farah Nazeer on the new frontlines of the sexual violence crisis

author: Matthew Kenyon
description:
Along the coasts of the Netherlands, Germany and Denmark, its intertidal flats host a wealth of marine life and birds. But extraction industries, tourism and fishing are taking their toll

Stand on the coastline at high tide and you look out over unbroken water, with sandy islands rising a few miles offshore. A few hours later and the view across the Wadden Sea has transformed into a maze of deep channels, drying sandbanks, salt marshes and mud flats.

As the largest unbroken system of intertidal sand and mud flats in the world, this ever-changing habitat stretches hundreds of miles along the north European coasts of Germany, Denmark and the Netherlands and was awarded world heritage status by Unesco in 2009.

Aerial view of the unique features of the Wadden Sea coast. Photograph: Janis Meyer/CWSS
title: Europe’s Wadden Sea is a natural wonder. So why might it join the world heritage in danger list?

author: Denis Campbell and Hanad Ahmed
description:
NHS chiefs said last year that 43% of maternity and neonatal units in England do not meet safety standards

Ministers have been accused of “gambling with the safety of mothers and babies” after admitting they do not know how much repairing decrepit maternity units would cost.

NHS chiefs said last year that shoddy infrastructure meant 43% of maternity and neonatal units in England did not meet basic safety standards. Infrastructure problems hampered the delivery of clinical care thousands of times every year, NHS England said.

Continue reading...
title: Ministers accused of ‘gambling with safety’ for not knowing cost of NHS maternity unit repairs

author: Cath Clarke
description:
She has a rare debilitating skin condition but still tackled a marathon, helped by her old friend. As new film The Slightest Touch tells the full story of that emotional day, its stars talk about their lifelong bond – and why he opened up about parenthood

Last month, HBO sent a private jet to Dublin to fly the star of a new documentary to London for the premiere. Colin Farrell appears in the film. But the private jet was not for him. The VIP passenger was Emma Fogarty, who has a rare, incurable genetic skin condition, epidermolysis bullosa or EB. Taking a commercial flight would have been physically impossible for her. As a publicist working on the film whispered to me, it was the one time you can emit all that carbon with a clean conscience.

Fogarty was born 42 years ago. When she was diagnosed with EB, her parents were told she was unlikely to survive a week – which was probably for the best, said the doctor. With EB, the proteins that hold the layers of skin together
title: ‘I’m a smalltown girl with a terrible disability. He’s a Hollywood superstar. But we’ve been laughing since we met’: Emma Fogarty and Colin Farrell on their extraordinary story

author: Geoffrey Bunting
description:
Disarmingly thoughtful stillness is the order of the day in the latest season of this Japanese show about a Tokyo eatery. What a shame it feels buried under other content

The first time we see the Master (Kaoru Kobayashi) in the sixth season of Midnight Diner, he cuts a curiously morose figure. His usually bustling establishment – open from midnight to 7am – is empty. No one, he notes, will come: Covid-19 keeps them at home. An ironic start for a drama arriving after a seven-year absence, delayed in part by uncertainty over the pandemic’s impact on small eateries.

The show’s return isn’t a shock. Based on Yarō Abe’s long-running manga, it has been a TV fixture in Japan since 2009. Netflix has just quietly released it, buried by the platform’s seeming aversion to marketing non-English series, which has swallowed reams of remarkable Japanese television.
title: Midnight Diner: Netflix just dropped its most beautiful show in years … and it’s barely been noticed

author: Sam Jones in Madrid
description:
Country’s sixth general election in 11 years could lead to far-right role in government for first time since Franco’s death

Spaniards head to the polls on 29 November to vote in the country’s sixth general election in 11 years. The snap election could end eight years of socialist-led rule and bring a far-right party into government for the first time since Spain’s return to democracy after the death of Gen Franco.

Continue reading...
title: Will Spain’s snap election in November bring a far-right party into government?

author: Associated Press
description:
Ahead of Apec summit, PM says ‘Canada is going to move forward either way’ when asked if Chinese investment was leverage in US negotiations

The prime minister of Canada, Mark Carney, said the country could turn to Chinese automakers if trade negotiations with the US president, Donald Trump, failed to preserve an integrated North American auto industry.

Carney’s comments in Cambodia on Monday came ahead of a planned meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping this week in Shenzhen, China, where auto manufacturing is expected to be discussed. The two leaders reached an agreement in January allowing tens of thousands of Chinese electric vehicles into Canada at reduced tariffs.

Continue reading...
title: Canada could work with Chinese automakers if US trade talks fail, says Carney

author: Guardian sport
description:
• Teenager’s ISA World Surfing Games win earns extra place at LA Games

  • Compatriot Ethan Ewing also wins gold at men’s event in Peru

Australian surfing prodigy Leihani Zoric’s meteoric rise appears to have no bounds after the 14-year-old upstaged a star-studded field at the ISA World Surfing Games to claim individual gold and earn her team a crucial boost ahead of the 2028 LA Olympics.

Zoric, who only turned 14 earlier this month, became the youngest champion in the tournament’s history after getting the better of a wealth of more experienced surfers at the event in Peru.

Continue reading...
title: Leihani Zoric, 14, stuns surfing world with gold medal to give Australia Olympic boost

Victoria police allege man, suspected of being a chapter president of the gang, sent ‘threats and harassing text messages’ to Nine journalist

A senior Hells Angel has been charged with threatening to kill Nine’s investigative reporter Nick McKenzie, the Victorian police taskforce investigating corruption in the building sector has confirmed.

Police said detectives from the taskforce had charged a man on Monday, after he “sent a number of allegedly threatening, offensive and abusive text messages” to the Age journalist on Friday.

author: Krishani Dhanji
description:
The Alfred hospital in Melbourne confirmed on Monday the independent MP had been discharged

Independent Australian MP Helen Haines has been discharged from hospital, four weeks after she was allegedly attacked by a man outside her electorate office in regional Victoria and lost both of her legs.

The Alfred hospital in Melbourne confirmed on Monday Haines had been discharged, but provided no further detail. Her office has been contacted.

Continue reading...
title: MP Helen Haines leaves hospital four weeks after alleged attack and double leg amputation

author: Associated Press
description:
Large waves up to 50ft flooded southern California streets and prompted evacuation warning near coastal city

The California coast was pummeled again on Sunday by huge waves that inundated beaches, flooded local streets and forced the closure of popular piers.

The National Weather Service office for the San Francisco Bay Area warned that surf up to 35ft (11 meters) was possible, along with dangerous rip currents and sneaker waves.

Continue reading...
title: Huge waves pummel California coast, forcing closure of popular piers
